question: What is the main job of the myelin sheath around a nerve fiber?

options.A: To produce the neurotransmitters needed for muscle contraction
options.B: To supply the nerve fiber with fresh oxygenated blood
options.C: To insulate the axon and help electrical impulses travel faster
options.D: To anchor the nerve securely to nearby bones and joints

explanation: Think of myelin like the plastic coating on an electrical wire! It helps nerve signals zip along much faster and more efficiently.

question: A patient reports numbness and tingling in their fingers after sleeping with their arm draped awkwardly over a chair. Which nerve function is primarily affected here?
explanation: Numbness and tingling are sensory symptoms caused by temporary pressure on sensory nerve fibers carrying touch and position information. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h1)

question: What is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide?
explanation: When blood sugar stays high over a long time, it slowly damages the tiny blood vessels that feed our nerves. That's why diabetes is the top cause of neuropathy!

question: A patient presents with symmetrical numbness and a 'stocking-glove' tingling pattern in both feet and hands. Which classification of neuropathy best fits this clinical picture?
explanation: Widespread, symmetrical involvement that starts in the extremities and moves inward is the classic presentation of a systemic polyneuropathy. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h2)

question: What happens to the nerve in a mild injury called neurapraxia?

options.A: The axon stays intact while the myelin sheath suffers temporary damage
options.B: The blood supply to the nerve is permanently cut off, causing rapid cell death
options.C: Both the axon and the outer connective tissue sheaths are completely severed
options.D: The axon is crushed or cut while the outer connective tissue tube stays intact

explanation: Neurapraxia is just a temporary block—like a pinched nerve. The myelin takes a little hit, but the core axon stays safe and sound.

question: Why does recovery from an axonotmesis injury take many months to occur?

options.A: Inflammation must completely clear out of the central nervous system before peripheral signals are allowed to pass.
options.B: Specialized white blood cells must first convert the damaged myelin into functional scar tissue.
options.C: The body has to completely rebuild the surrounding bone structure before nerve fibers can begin to cross the gap.
options.D: The regrowing axon must slowly creep down the remaining connective tube at a rate of about one millimeter per day.

explanation: Axonal regeneration is a very slow biological process, requiring months for fibers to travel from the injury site all the way back to muscles in the feet or hands. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h3)

question: In diabetic neuropathy, how do we classify burning pain versus numbness?

options.A: Burning pain is an autonomic symptom, while numbness is a motor system deficit
options.B: Both burning pain and numbness are classified as positive motor symptoms
options.C: Both burning pain and numbness are classified as negative sensory symptoms
options.D: Burning pain is a positive sensory symptom, while numbness is a negative sensory symptom

explanation: Remember: 'positive' means the nervous system is adding an extra sensation (like pain or tingling), while 'negative' means a function is missing or lost (like numbness).

question: Which physical assessment finding is most characteristic of chronic motor nerve damage in the lower extremities?
explanation: When motor nerves stop stimulating leg muscles, the muscles shrink (atrophy), and the muscles lifting the front of the foot become too weak, leading to foot drop. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h4)

question: Which test checks the speed and strength of electrical signals in a peripheral nerve?
explanation: Nerve Conduction Studies use gentle, tiny electrical pulses on the skin to see how fast signals travel down the nerve highway.

question: A patient with suspected polyneuropathy has blood drawn for routine laboratory tests. Which underlying condition is the nurse primarily helping to screen for with tests like HbA1c?
explanation: Checking fasting blood sugar and HbA1c is a priority diagnostic step because diabetes is the leading cause of peripheral neuropathy. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h5)

question: Which type of medication is often prescribed to help manage chronic nerve pain?
explanation: Even though they were first made for seizures, anticonvulsants calm down wild, overactive nerve firing, making them great for shooting and burning nerve pain!

question: Why don't standard painkillers like ibuprofen work well for severe nerve pain?

options.A: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs only work when applied directly to the skin
options.B: Ibuprofen cannot cross the blood-brain barrier under any circumstances
options.C: Pain receptors in the peripheral nerves are completely immune to chemical blockers
options.D: Neuropathic pain is caused by abnormal nerve firing rather than general tissue inflammation

explanation: Ibuprofen fights swelling and tissue inflammation, but nerve pain comes from electrical misfires in the pathway itself. Different problem, different solution!

question: Why should a nurse teach a patient with diabetic foot neuropathy to test bathwater with their elbow instead of their feet?

options.A: Numbness in the feet prevents the patient from accurately sensing water temperature, risking scald burns
options.B: Elbow skin contains specialized sweat glands that neutralize toxic minerals found in tap water
options.C: Hot water causes immediate and permanent paralysis of the small motor nerves in the toes
options.D: The skin on the feet is biologically incapable of absorbing heat evenly compared to the upper body

explanation: Because neuropathy takes away normal feeling in the feet, patients might step into water that's way too hot without realizing it until they get burned. Using the elbow helps keep them safe!

question: What is the most important daily habit for preventing foot complications in a patient with nerve loss?

options.A: Inspecting the feet daily for cuts, blisters, and pressure injuries
options.B: Encouraging barefoot walking indoors to stimulate deep tendon reflexes
options.C: Massaging the toes vigorously with alcohol twice a day
options.D: Applying high-strength heating pads to the calves every evening

explanation: When you can't feel your feet, small cuts can turn into big, infected sores without you noticing. Daily checks catch little problems before they become emergencies!
